script:
Good morning. Here's your briefing for Saturday, September 26.

First up, AI & Tech.

A new paper from arXiv proposes an architecture called the Infinite-Parameter LLM. The core idea is to learn from live interactions by dynamically updating model weights, rather than just using a static context window. It uses a compact hypernetwork to turn online data into low-rank modulations of a base network, so weights are generated from live data instead of being read from memory. This approach aims to free the context window and persist updates across user sessions.

A new developer tool called Skillsync has launched out of YC Winter twenty-six. It’s designed to make AI chat sessions portable across different coding agents, acting as a universal converter for session files. This lets you move an entire session, including messages, reasoning, and tool calls, from one agent to another without starting over. The core is a local, open-source Rust engine called T-X-script, which the creators compare to ffmpeg for agent sessions.

A recent blog post argues that for classification tasks, an LLM's output should be treated as a feature, not the final verdict. The author notes that LLM classifiers are hard to calibrate and may ignore structured data. The proposed solution is to feed the LLM's label into a simple logistic regression model. This allows for proper calibration and threshold control using standard ML techniques, effectively using the LLM for feature engineering.

In competitive news, a Reuters headline states that Anthropic plans to combine its Claude AI features into a single interface and is launching new document tools.

OpenAI is expanding its advertising efforts with a program called Sponsored Agents.

A couple of other headlines with minimal detail have also appeared. One from Stanford Medicine claims that AI agents made from manuscripts can now communicate with each other to make new discoveries. Another headline from The Rundown AI reports that a co-creator of ChatGPT has launched a new kind of AI, though no further details were provided in the source.

Next, US Headlines.

Alabama has executed an inmate convicted of a 1998 double murder, following a Supreme Court decision that cleared the way for the lethal injection to proceed. The court had previously blocked the execution while a dispute over the inmate's request to be put to death by nitrogen gas was considered.

In Washington, the White House has withdrawn the nomination of Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as ICE. The move came after Republican Senator Markwayne Mullin reversed his support for the nominee, leaving the agency without a confirmed director for the foreseeable future.

Former President Donald Trump has suggested he might tear down the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts if reelected, stating he would replace it with something "much better." His comments add a political dimension to an ongoing legal dispute by preservationists over the cultural center's original design.

On the international front, former President Trump also stated the U.S. would not approve a deal for Canada to form a closer partnership with the European Union. Canada has been exploring the possibility of becoming an "associate member" of the EU, a move seen as a reaction to years of strained relations with the United States.

And finally, federal investigators have released a report on a Florida immigration facility nicknamed "Alligator Alcatraz," confirming that detainees were held in small outdoor cages. A former detainee testified to being confined for up to fifteen hours in what officials reportedly called "calming areas."

Turning to Immigration & Visas.

A new public charge rule for green card applicants is set to take effect on September eighteenth. The change clarifies how U S C I S determines if an applicant is likely to become dependent on government benefits when they apply for adjustment of status. Under the new policy, officials will not consider the use of most non-cash benefits, such as food assistance programs like SNAP, the Children's Health Insurance Program, most forms of Medicaid, or housing subsidies. This policy provides more clarity for green card applicants and their families about accessing critical health and nutrition services without affecting their immigration status.

And finally, Markets.

The major U.S. indices all finished in the green. The S&P 500 rose about one point one percent, while the Nasdaq led the way, gaining roughly one point seven percent. The Dow also added just over half a percent.

Looking at your watchlist, it was a strong day for the big tech names. Nvidia was the standout, up about two and a half percent, and Amazon gained just over two percent. Microsoft, Apple, and Google also saw solid gains, with each rising more than one percent.

That's your briefing. Have a great day.
